To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the optimal phenology and plant height of wheat genotypes is highly related to the temperatures and to rainfall at heading and that a set of genotypes with different PHs and phenologies is not beneficial.
winter wheat genotypes with later phenology and shorter plant height have lower grain yield in the studied areas of Turkey and that a diverse set of genotypes does not improve yield stability.

(1) wheat genotypes with different PHs and phenology are exposed to different weather conditions around the time of heading and that (2) the optimal phenology for winter wheat in rain fed environments is a short duration of 90 days.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new wheat lines for rain fed areas of Turkey and northern Iran, which are likely to be exposed to erratic weather patterns in the future.
the identification of wheat lines that are more resilient to erratic weather patterns in the face of climate change.
the optimization of winter wheat ideotype(s) for use as a reference in the calibration process of wheat selection in rain fed winter wheat production areas of Turkey and of Iran.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optimal wheat genotype should be early, tall, and drought avoidant.
wheat breeders should aim for a narrow range of phenology and height to increase resilience to erratic and unpredictable weather patterns.
a wheat line with optimal phenology and height is suggested to be used for selection decisions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a single wheat genotype (with optimal phenology and height) may serve as a testing line for use in selection calibration decisions.
the optimal winter wheat ideotype for the study areas is early, with a PH of 80 cm, and with an optimal heading time around 15 April, which would be the best choice for a testing line.
the optimal phenology of wheat lines is highly correlated with the temperature and rainfall at which winter wheats are exposed around heading time.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the optimal phenology and PH of wheat genotypes are highly related to the weather conditions they are exposed to around heading time, and that the optimal phenologies of genotypes are highly dependent on the location and year of testing.
the selection of a single wheat line with optimal PH and heading time may be the most appropriate strategy for breeding programs aiming to increase wheat resilience to climate change.
the selection of winter wheat genotypes with a narrow range of phenology and PH is more likely to be beneficial in terms of GY than a set of diverse phenology and PH genotypes.
